question: According to the principles agreed at Chicago, how is the continuing airworthiness of an aircraft to be ensured?

options.text: By a new type certificate every year
By the continued validity of its certificate of airworthiness
By an inspection by the State of Design whenever the aircraft changes owner or operator
By the operator's own declaration before each flight

explanation: Each aeroplane has a certificate stating it was airworthy when built, and continued validation of that certificate ensures its continuing airworthiness. The type certificate concerns the design, not each aircraft's ongoing state.

question: Which State issues the type certificate for a new aeroplane type after design and flight testing?

options.text: The State of Design (manufacture)
The State of Registry of each aircraft
The State of the first operator
Every State in which the type will be operated, each issuing its own type certificate

explanation: The State of Design/Manufacture issues the type certificate once testing is complete; it then applies to subsequent production aircraft. Each individual aircraft's C of A is issued by its State of Registry.

question: A manufacturer produces a much modified version of an existing type. What may the certifying authorities require?

options.text: Nothing; the original type certificate covers all variants automatically
Only a new noise certificate, as the airworthiness of the original type still applies
Only a new registration mark
Re-certification, if they judge it is no longer the same aeroplane

explanation: The original type certificate covers later marks within reason, but authorities may decide a variant is effectively a different aeroplane (as with the 747-400) and require re-certification.

question: Under what document does a prototype fly during initial flight testing?

options.text: A certificate of airworthiness issued by the State of Registry
A special VFR clearance from the local air traffic unit valid for the test programme
A permit to fly issued by the State of Manufacture
A type certificate issued in advance

explanation: Before certification the prototype flies under a permit to fly issued by the State of Manufacture; the type certificate follows successful testing.

question: How do Annex 8 and Annex 6 relate to each other on airworthiness?

options.text: Annex 8 replaces Annex 6 for aeroplanes over 5700 kg
They are complementary: Annex 8 engineering, Annex 6 operational standards
They are unrelated: Annex 6 deals only with licensing and Annex 8 only with registration marks
Annex 6 covers engineering standards; Annex 8 only the certificate's format

explanation: Airworthiness is not fully defined by Annex 8 alone: Annex 8 deals with it from the engineering viewpoint, Annex 6 with the safety standards needed for operations (performance and limitations). They complement each other.

question: The airworthiness standards of Annex 8 Part III apply to aeroplanes with a certificated maximum take-off mass of more than:

options.text: 5700 kg, used for any commercial or private flight
2250 kg, used for any purpose
5700 kg, intended for international carriage of passengers, cargo or mail
136 000 kg, the heavy wake turbulence category

explanation: Part III applies to aeroplanes over 5700 kg MTOM intended for carriage of passengers, cargo or mail in international air navigation (with at least two engines).

question: For the Annex 8 Part III standards to apply, the aeroplane must also have:

options.text: At least two engines
A pressurised cabin
At least 20 passenger seats
A flight crew of at least two pilots and a flight engineer

explanation: The Part III standards apply to aeroplanes over 5700 kg for international carriage that have at least two engines.

question: Unless specifically exempted, the airworthiness standards apply to:

options.text: The cabin and the emergency equipment only, the rest being covered by the operator
The engines and propellers only
The airframe only
The complete aeroplane, including power units, systems and equipment

explanation: The standards apply to the complete aeroplane, including its power units, systems and equipment.

question: In Europe, the detailed airworthiness standards equivalent to the Annex 8 requirements are published as:

options.text: Joint operating requirements
Acceptable Means of Compliance only
Aeronautical information circulars issued by each member State
Certification Specifications (CS)

explanation: The European equivalent is the Certification Specifications (CS), such as CS-25 for large aeroplanes.

question: Which State issues the certificate of airworthiness for an individual aircraft?

options.text: The State of Registry
The State of Manufacture
The State of Design
The State of the operator, if different from the State of Registry

explanation: The C of A is issued by the State of Registry when satisfactory evidence shows the aircraft complies with the appropriate airworthiness requirements.

question: Which item is included in the standard certificate of airworthiness form?

options.text: The name of the pilot-in-command
The aircraft serial number
The owner's name and address
The aircraft's maximum number of passengers for each flight

explanation: The standard C of A shows nationality and registration marks, manufacturer and designation, aircraft serial number and categories/operation. The owner's name and address appear on the certificate of registration.

question: Who is responsible for determining whether an aircraft continues to be airworthy?

options.text: The State of Design
The State in which the aircraft is currently operating
The State of Registry
The manufacturer

explanation: The State of Registry determines continuing airworthiness. The State of Design has duties such as the structural integrity programme.

question: For aircraft over 5700 kg, the State of Registry must maintain a system for recording:

options.text: All flights made by each aircraft
Changes of ownership only, with the dates on which they took place and the new owner's address
Faults, malfunctions, defects or other occurrences that might affect airworthiness
All crew members who have flown each aircraft

explanation: The State of Registry keeps a system for recording faults, malfunctions, defects and other occurrences that might affect the airworthiness of aircraft over 5700 kg.

question: Which State must ensure that a structural integrity programme, including corrosion control, exists for aircraft over 5700 kg?

options.text: The State of the operator
The State where the aircraft is maintained, whatever its registration
The State of Registry
The State of Design

explanation: The State of Design ensures a structural integrity programme, including corrosion control information, exists for the type.

question: A certificate of airworthiness remains valid, or is renewed, provided that:

options.text: The owner pays an annual fee to the Organization
Continued airworthiness is confirmed by periodic inspection at intervals set by the State
The aircraft flies at least once a month
No incident or accident has been reported to the State during the previous twelve months of operation

explanation: The C of A remains valid or is renewed if continued airworthiness is determined by periodic inspection; the interval is established by the State.

question: An aircraft is damaged. Who judges whether it is still airworthy and specifies the repairs needed?

options.text: The State of Registry
The State where the damage occurred
The insurance company that covers the aircraft
The State of Design

explanation: The State of Registry judges whether the damage makes the aircraft unairworthy, specifies the necessary repairs and checks they were done before re-issuing the C of A.

question: Where are an aircraft's approved operating limitations defined?

options.text: In the operator's air operator certificate, issued by the State of the operator for each type
In the AIP of the State of Registry
In the certificate of registration
In the flight manual (or other approved means) carried for the aircraft

explanation: Each aircraft must have a flight manual (or other means) defining the approved limitations and the information needed for safe operation.

question: If an aircraft's limiting speeds are specified as Mach numbers, the aircraft must be fitted with:

options.text: A radio altimeter
A Machmeter
A second airspeed indicator
An outside air temperature gauge with a Mach conversion table

explanation: Where limiting speeds are expressed as a Mach number, the aircraft must be fitted with a Machmeter.

question: When a State first enters an aircraft on its register and issues or validates its certificate of airworthiness, it must inform:

options.text: The previous owner
The Organization's regional office
The State of Design
Every State the aircraft is expected to overfly in the following year

explanation: A State first registering an aircraft and issuing or validating its C of A must inform the State of Design, which can then pass on continuing airworthiness information.
